concepts.name: Matching initial server and client output

questions.prompt: A server already sent React-generated HTML. Which API connects the client React tree to it?

choices.text: hydrateRoot, using the server container and matching initial tree.
useEffect, which attaches React handlers without a hydration root.
createRoot, which automatically reuses and hydrates all existing server markup.
root.render alone, which automatically infers the original server component tree.

questions.explanation: Hydration reuses server HTML and attaches React behavior. It is distinct from creating all markup on the client.

sources.title: hydrateRoot
sources.claim: hydrateRoot attaches React to server-generated HTML, requires identical initial client and server output, treats mismatches as bugs and can switch to client rendering if root.render is called before hydration finishes.

questions.prompt: What is the primary distinction between server HTML rendering and hydration?

choices.text: Server rendering requires the browser to execute every Effect first.
Hydration generates all HTML exclusively on the server after a click.
Server HTML contains every client event handler as executable attributes.
Hydration attaches client React behavior to existing server-rendered HTML.

questions.explanation: The server produces HTML; hydration makes that markup participate in the client React application.

sources.claim: hydrateRoot attaches React to server-generated HTML, requires identical initial client and server output, treats mismatches as bugs and can switch to client rendering if root.render is called before hydration finishes.

questions.prompt: The server renders 10:00 but the client first render independently computes 10:01. What is the issue?

choices.text: No issue, because React guarantees patching every mismatch identically.
The browser automatically changes server timestamps to client time.
Initial output differs, violating the hydration matching requirement.
No issue, because text never participates in hydration checks.

questions.explanation: Initial output must match. Pass shared initial data or use a deliberate post-hydration update rather than mismatching independently.

questions.prompt: Which strategy avoids a browser-only flag causing initial hydration differences?

choices.text: Set the client initial output differently to force a replacement.
Read window during server rendering and assume it always exists.
Hide all mismatch warnings without checking the resulting behavior.
Render matching initial content and update browser-only state in an Effect.

questions.explanation: The documented two-pass pattern first matches server content, then changes state after client hydration.

questions.prompt: Where does useEffect setup execute in server-rendered React?

choices.text: Only on the server, because hydration forbids external synchronization.
On both sides, always before HTML can be generated.
Only on the client; it does not run during server rendering.
On neither side when hydrateRoot attaches the application.

questions.explanation: Effects are client-only. Render output needed for server HTML cannot depend on an Effect having executed.

sources.title: useEffect
sources.claim: Effects only run on the client and do not run during server rendering.

questions.prompt: What can happen if root.render is called before hydrateRoot finishes hydrating?

choices.text: React ignores every root.render call made before hydration completes.
React queues every early root.render until hydration preserves the full server tree.
React guarantees the update is invisible until every server node matches.
React clears existing server HTML and switches to client rendering.

questions.explanation: The API documents switching to client rendering in this case, losing the expected reuse of server HTML.

questions.prompt: Which hydration claims are accurate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Server HTML automatically makes client event handlers unnecessary.
The initial React tree should correspond to the server markup.
Hydration allows the page to become an interactive React application.
Hydration attaches React to HTML already produced on the server.
Hydration is just the browser painting an ordinary static document.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: client behavior must be connected. B: Correct: matching is a requirement. C: Correct: event behavior is activated on the client. D: Correct: existing markup is reused. E: Incorrect: React attachment and painting are different operations.

questions.prompt: Which practices help prevent hydration mismatches? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assume React will patch every mismatching attribute automatically.
Use shared server-provided data for the first client render.
Use suppression to avoid investigating all structural differences.
Compute independent random first-render values on both sides.
Treat unexpected initial mismatches as bugs to investigate.

questions.explanation: A: Incorrect: there are no guarantees all differences are patched. B: Correct: consistent data gives consistent initial output. C: Incorrect: suppression is a narrow escape hatch, not general repair. D: Incorrect: independent values can differ. E: Correct: the documentation says to fix mismatches.

questions.prompt: Which statements follow from client-only Effects? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Effect setup cannot supply values already required by the server render.
An Effect with an empty dependency list can provide the initial server-rendered state.
Adding [] makes an Effect execute on both server and client.
A client Effect can update browser-dependent state after initial hydration.
External synchronization through useEffect runs in the client environment.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: server HTML must come from available render inputs. B: Incorrect: Effects do not execute on the server, even with an empty dependency list. C: Incorrect: dependency syntax does not change the execution environment. D: Correct: a post-hydration pass can update state. E: Correct: the API explicitly limits Effects to clients.

sources.title: useEffect
sources.claim: Effects do not run during server rendering; client Effects can synchronize and update state after the initial render.

questions.prompt: Which hydrateRoot lifecycle claims are documented? Select all that apply.

choices.text: An early root.render can discard server HTML and use client rendering.
After hydration, root.render can update the client React tree.
hydrateRoot expects the same initial output as the server.
Calling root.render before hydration always preserves the full server tree.
Calling root.render before hydration only attaches events and can never replace markup.

questions.explanation: A: Correct: early updates can switch rendering mode. B: Correct: the root supports subsequent client updates. C: Correct: identical initial output is required. D: Incorrect: server markup may be cleared. E: Incorrect: an early call can clear server HTML and switch to client rendering.
